opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things that seems like a pedantic detail but actually matters a lot once you start training AIs.

The rules most humans play by, especially Japanese rules, have a step at the end of the game that's essentially social. Both players stop, look at the board, and agree on which groups are "dead," meaning stones that can't avoid capture no matter what. Those get removed and counted as prisoners without anyone playing it out. A strong human looks at a group sitting inside your territory with no way to make two eyes and just says, "that's dead." If there's a dispute, there are procedures for resolving it hypothetically, but it relies a lot on shared understanding of what's obviously settled.

Tromp-Taylor rules are designed to be completely mechanical, with no judgment involved. The game ends when both players pass in succession. Then you score by area: your stones on the board, plus any empty points that only touch your color. There's no "agreeing" that something is dead. If a stone is still on the board at the end, it counts. So if your opponent has a hopeless little group sitting in your territory and you never actually capture it, it breaks up your territory, because those empty points now touch both colors. There are some other technical choices too, like positional superko and allowing suicide moves, but the dead-stone thing is the big one.

That makes Tromp-Taylor really nice for computers. You can write the scoring function in a few lines, there's no ambiguity, and you can hand it straight to a self-play reinforcement learning loop as a clean reward signal. You don't need a separate model to judge life and death.

But it creates this gap between what the AI is good at and what the scoring actually rewards. The famous example is the adversarial policy work against KataGo from a few years back. They found a really weak-looking adversary that could beat a superhuman Go AI, not by outplaying it, but by exploiting the end of the game. The adversary would build some stones in the victim's territory, and the victim, thinking intuitively like a human ("I'm clearly winning, that stuff is dead"), would pass. Then the adversary passes, the game ends, and under strict Tromp-Taylor scoring those "dead" stones count, so the adversary wins. Any human would look at that and say the victim obviously won, but under the literal rules it lost.

So for me the interesting lesson is about specification. The human rules encode a lot of tacit understanding, and the machine rules strip that out to get something precise. Then you discover your agent learned a policy that was a great approximation of "playing Go well" in the human sense, but wasn't actually robust to the exact objective you wrote down. It's a nice small-scale example of the gap between what we mean and what we specify, which shows up everywhere in AI.

r001.rationale: The response says Tromp-Taylor rules are mechanical and unambiguous, and explains that this makes them useful for computer scoring and self-play.

r002.rationale: It says Tromp-Taylor allows suicide moves, but does not state that typical human rules prohibit them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short version is that Tromp-Taylor is what you get when you try to write down Go in a way a computer can't argue with, and the human rulesets are what you get when a couple thousand years of players agreed on conventions that work fine as long as both sides are reasonable people.

The actual game play is essentially identical. Where they diverge is at the end. Under Japanese rules, when both players pass, you look at the board and you just agree on what's dead. There's a group sitting in your territory that's obviously not going to live, and you both nod and remove it without playing it out. That's great for humans, because it saves a lot of tedious moves, but it relies on shared judgment. If you and I disagree about whether a group is dead, the Japanese rules have this whole appendix of special cases, and historically there were actual disputes that had to go to committees.

Tromp-Taylor just refuses to have that conversation. Nothing is dead unless it's actually captured. When the game ends, you score by area, which is your stones plus the empty points that only reach your stones. If you think my group is dead, you have to go kill it. And filling in your own territory to do that doesn't cost you anything under area scoring, whereas under Japanese territory scoring every move inside your own territory loses you a point. So the rules are designed so that the "obvious" move of just finishing things off is free, and the whole thing becomes a function you can evaluate with no human in the loop.

For training AlphaGo or KataGo or any of these systems, that's the property you need. Self-play generates millions of games, and you need a scoring function that returns a number every time, with no ambiguity and no judgment calls. Tromp-Taylor also has superko, so you can't cycle forever, which matters when you have two agents who will absolutely find infinite loops if you let them.

The interesting consequence is that this leaks into the behavior. An AI trained under Tromp-Taylor will sometimes play these moves at the end that look weird or even rude to a human, like filling in dame or capturing stones that any club player would just take off the board. It's not that the model doesn't understand the position. It's that under its rules, the group really isn't dead until the stones are gone, and there's no penalty for being thorough. And then there's the flip side, which we saw with the adversarial attacks on KataGo. People found that if you build a weird cyclic group inside the AI's territory, the AI will pass thinking it's winning, and under strict Tromp-Taylor scoring that group is alive and the AI loses. A human would never pass there, partly because a human would just keep playing until it was settled.

So I think of it as the usual story with formalizing anything. You trade away flexibility and shared understanding for something that's machine-checkable, and most of the time the gap is invisible. But then you hit edge cases where the formal version and the intuitive version disagree, and that's exactly where the system does something strange. It's a pretty clean toy example of the general problem of specifying what you actually want.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that Tromp-Taylor is a way of specifying Go that’s particularly clean for a computer. You can play the game out and determine the score from the board, without needing the players to agree about which groups are dead.

In human play, we usually skip that last bit. Both players recognize that a group is dead, so we remove it rather than make someone actually capture it. Human rules also vary—Japanese and Chinese scoring, for example, aren’t identical—so it’s not quite one AI rule set versus one human rule set.

The interesting distinction is that something humans treat as obvious can still require an explicit procedure in the formal rules. Usually those give you the same outcome, but you have to be careful about assuming that they always do.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that Tromp-Taylor is a very clean, mathematical formulation of Go. You score the stones on the board plus the empty points surrounded by your stones, and you prohibit moves that repeat a previous board position. It’s convenient for a computer because you can determine the outcome directly from the board.

Human rules, especially Japanese rules, involve things like agreeing on which stones are dead and counting territory and prisoners. There’s a little more procedure around ending the game. Under Tromp-Taylor, you can just play out a disputed position and capture the stones. Filling in your own territory generally doesn’t cost you points, because you’re replacing an empty point you owned with a stone you own.

So it’s mostly the same strategic game, but the scoring and some edge cases differ. And humans also play with area-scoring rules, so it’s not a strict AI-versus-human distinction.
